chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from his father, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from Mu'tab who said:

When Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) had dinner, he said to me: 'When you enter the storage, seek out for me two (lumps of) sugar.' So I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you! There is nothing there.' So he said, 'Enter, woe be unto you!' So I entered and found two (lumps of) sugar, so came with these to him.

key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: May I be sacrificed for you (a phrase of respect)

ai.seo_question: What does the story of Imam al-Sadiq and the two lumps of sugar demonstrate about his knowledge?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the Imam’s precise knowledge of his household’s inventory, often interpreted by Shia scholars as a sign of *‘Ilm al-Ghaib* (knowledge of the unseen) granted by God or a result of meticulous stewardship. The specific mention of 'sugar' (sukkar) is significant as it reflects the luxury and distinct dietary habits of the Ahl al-Bayt during the Abbasid era, serving as a tangible marker of their status and divine favor. The narrative underscores the Imam’s authority over his material possessions, reinforcing the concept of his comprehensive knowledge extending to even the smallest details of his domestic life.
